attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, in his own voice. He is not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: This is a present-tense observation about the roughly two years before the post. The normalisation keeps the exclusivity and burn parts. It reasonably leaves out the rhetorical 'nobody can really describe' and treats 'killer apps' as meaning industry-defining products.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair. 'Industry-defining' has no threshold, and the burn statement needs figures for ChatGPT alone, not OpenAI as a whole, because Zitron named the product. The result depends on how 'industry-defining' is read and on how costs are split between ChatGPT and the rest of OpenAI. Zitron supplied neither.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own disclosure, dated 2024-10-18. GitHub Copilot is a credible rival product, but Microsoft is describing itself, and subscriber counts alone do not show it was industry-defining. The exclusivity claim is neither settled nor refuted.

Epoch AI estimate published 2025-10-10, before the cutoff. It gives gross compute spending for all of OpenAI in 2024, partly projected. It does not isolate ChatGPT's net burn, and the period does not match the one claimed.

reviews.rationale: Copilot adoption figures come from Microsoft itself and do not show that Copilot met an 'industry-defining' standard. That leaves the exclusivity claim unsettled. The only financial evidence is an estimate of OpenAI-wide gross compute spending, with no figures for ChatGPT alone. Under the contract, that can neither support nor contradict the claim that ChatGPT burns billions. The packet cannot settle either part of the claim.
